question: What is the upper limit for BufferMinutes?
context: AC-1 requires validation '>= 0 with a reasonable upper limit' but neither the story nor the code defines the limit. The value becomes a constant in the handler, a `maximum` in the API contract, and the boundary values of the AC-1 tests.

code_says.claim: No validator library; Resources validates inline in handlers and throws ResourcesDomainException, mapped to HTTP 400 with body { Errors: [ { Code, Message } ] }.
The only integer range rule in Resources is a Math.Clamp on pagination (MinTake=1, MaxTake=50) — it clamps instead of rejecting.
The upper limit is not defined anywhere in the codebase or the story text.

options.label: 1440 (24 h)
options.consequences: A buffer is turnaround time between bookings; anything longer than a day is unavailability, not a buffer. Constant BufferMinutesMax = 1440; tests use 1441 as the first rejected value.

options.label: 10080 (7 days)
options.consequences: Covers multi-day turnaround (rental gear service, weekly cottage turnover). Constant = 10080; tests use 10081.

options.label: No upper limit (int.MaxValue)
options.consequences: Only '>= 0' is enforced. Contradicts the AC wording ('reasonable upper limit'); Availability would have to guard against absurd values itself.

recommendation: 1440 (24 h) — a buffer models cleaning/turnaround between two bookings; 24 h is the largest value that still reads as a buffer rather than a blackout period, and raising it later is a one-constant change plus one test value.
argument_against: Some resources genuinely need multi-day turnaround (equipment sent for servicing, cottages with weekly changeover); with 1440 the owner of such a group cannot express that and would have to model it as unavailability in Availability, which does not exist yet. 10080 costs nothing extra today.
consequences: spec FR for validation, AC-1 boundary values, `maximum` in contract-delta.overlay.json for CreateResourceTypeRequest/UpdateResourceTypeRequest, one constant in the Resources handlers.
withdrawn_reason: DEC-3: Availability owns the buffer; BufferMinutes leaves this story.

question: How should the migration initialise BufferMinutes on existing resource types?
context: Adding BufferMinutes to ResourceType requires a new EF migration in Resources.Migrations (the fourth; last one is 20260514155140_AddResourceTypeUniqueAndCursorIndexes). Existing rows in resources.resource_types need a value. This is on the owner's hard list (data & migrations) so it is never defaulted by an agent.

code_says.claim: ResourceType has no BufferMinutes property; table resource_types, schema resources.
Within one story a module has a single migration (constitution Art. VI).
AC-1 says BufferMinutes defaults to 0 when omitted and is an int.

options.label: NOT NULL, default 0 for existing rows
options.consequences: Column `buffer_minutes integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`; existing schemas behave as if the owner set 0 (no buffer). Entity property is `int`. Matches AC-1 literally.

options.label: Nullable column (NULL = not set)
options.consequences: Column `buffer_minutes integer NULL`; existing schemas have NULL, which Availability could treat as 'not configured'. Entity property becomes `int?`, events carry `int?`, AC-1 wording ('int, default 0') must change.

recommendation: NOT NULL, default 0 for existing rows — it is exactly what AC-1 states, it keeps the event contract simple (`int BufferMinutes`), and today no consumer distinguishes 'unset' from 0.
argument_against: A NOT NULL 0 erases the information that the owner never chose a buffer; if Availability later wants a group-level default buffer that applies when the schema has none, NULL would have carried that meaning for free and a second migration will be needed.
consequences: Migration AddBufferMinutesToResourceType; entity/command/result types; event payload type; AC-1 test for an existing schema returned by GET with BufferMinutes = 0.
withdrawn_reason: DEC-3: Availability owns the buffer; BufferMinutes leaves this story.

question: Epic open decision no. 3: which module owns the schema buffer (BufferMinutes)?
context: The story lists Created and Deleted events only. ResourceSchemaCreatedEvent carries BufferMinutes, so Availability will cache it. If the owner later edits the buffer via PUT /resources/types/{id}, nothing tells Availability — its copy goes stale, which defeats the goal 'read models without cross-module queries'. The story front matter marks epic decision no. 3 (Resources vs Availability as source of truth) as still open; the answer determines whether BufferMinutes belongs on ResourceType at all. Round 1 follow-up: the owner asked for a full ownership analysis; the recommendation was revised from Resources-master to Availability-owner (see round-1.md).

code_says.claim: PUT /resources/types/{id} exists and replaces Name/Description/PropertyDefinitions; no event is published today anywhere in Resources.
No Availability module exists; Shared.Abstractions/Events has only ManagementGroups/ and Users/.
ManagementGroups publishes after SaveChangesAsync: group.Delete(); SaveChangesAsync(); PublishAsync(new GroupDeleted(...)).
ResourceType carries no time/scheduling semantics today (Id, GroupId, Name, Description, timestamps, PropertyDefinitions).
Epic decision no. 2 (owner-provided story text) says deleting a schema hard-deletes ITS RULES, implying Availability keeps rules keyed by SchemaId.

options.label: Availability owns the buffer - rescope this story to lifecycle events only
options.consequences: AC-1 and AC-2 are removed; ResourceSchemaCreatedEvent becomes (Guid SchemaId, Guid GroupId); no BufferMinutes column, request or GET change in Resources; BufferMinutes is defined later as a per-schema rule inside the Availability module (defaults created on ResourceSchemaCreatedEvent). DEC-1 and DEC-2 are withdrawn. Issue #10 title/AC must be updated by the business layer.

options.label: Resources owns the buffer + ResourceSchemaUpdatedEvent
options.consequences: BufferMinutes lives on ResourceType; PUT publishes ResourceSchemaUpdatedEvent(Guid SchemaId, Guid GroupId, int BufferMinutes) after SaveChangesAsync; new AC-8; Availability caches the value. DEC-1 and DEC-2 stay open.

options.label: Resources owns the buffer, no update event in this story
options.consequences: Story exactly as issued; PUT changes the buffer silently and the Availability cache drifts until a later story adds the event.

options.label: RETURN to the business session
options.consequences: verdict.json = RETURN with this analysis; the story is re-shaped in session A before any spec is written.

recommendation: Availability owns the buffer - rescope this story to lifecycle events only. The buffer is a scheduling rule with exactly one consumer; epic decision no. 2 already assumes Availability keeps rules per SchemaId; keeping it in Resources creates two sources of truth and a permanent sync mechanism (Updated event + handler) for a value Resources never uses. Future rules (opening hours, min/max duration) would otherwise pile up on ResourceType.
argument_against: Availability does not exist yet, so the buffer is delayed until that module is built; the user-facing model "a schema has a default buffer" is simplest when the field sits on the schema and its form; issue #10 was written around Resources and must be re-shaped, and the schema form would have to talk to two modules.
consequences: Option 1: story.md loses AC-1/AC-2, AC-3 payload changes, DEC-1/DEC-2 withdrawn, spec covers 4 lifecycle events + DEC-5 soft delete. Option 2: AC-8 added, 5th event record. Option 4: verdict.json RETURN.
chosen: Availability owns the buffer - rescope this story to lifecycle events only

question: When a schema is deleted and its instances are soft-deleted in bulk, which events are published?
context: DeleteResourceTypeCommandHandler soft-deletes all instances of the type with one bulk SQL statement and then hard-deletes the type. AC-5 requires a ResourceSchemaDeletedEvent; AC-6 requires ResourceInstanceDeletedEvent when an instance is deleted through its own command. The story does not say whether instances deleted as a side effect of schema deletion get their own events.

code_says.claim: DeleteResourceTypeCommandHandler: (1) SoftDeleteInstancesAsync via ExecuteUpdateAsync (bulk, no entities loaded), (2) Remove type, (3) single SaveChangesAsync.
ResourceInstanceCreatedEvent(ResourceId, SchemaId) gives the consumer the instance→schema link (AC-4).
GroupDeletedHandler bulk-deletes types via ExecuteDeleteAsync; per-schema events there are explicitly out of scope.

options.label: Only ResourceSchemaDeletedEvent; consumer cascades by SchemaId
options.consequences: One event per schema deletion: ResourceSchemaDeletedEvent(Guid SchemaId, Guid GroupId). Availability must delete everything it holds for that SchemaId (rules and instance read models). Bulk SQL in the handler stays as is.

options.label: Schema event + one ResourceInstanceDeletedEvent per instance
options.consequences: Handler must load instance ids first (or keep the bulk update and query ids), then publish N+1 events after SaveChangesAsync. Availability gets explicit per-instance signals; more events, more tests, and a group with many instances produces a burst.

recommendation: Only ResourceSchemaDeletedEvent; consumer cascades by SchemaId — the epic rule already says 'deleting a schema hard-deletes its rules', i.e. the consumer is expected to cascade from the schema; the consumer knows instance→schema from ResourceInstanceCreatedEvent; and it keeps the existing bulk delete path untouched.
argument_against: Cascading by SchemaId pushes a delete-consistency rule into a module that does not exist yet; if Availability's read models are keyed only by ResourceId, per-instance events are the simpler, more explicit contract and avoid a partially-cascaded state if the consumer's cascade fails half-way.
consequences: ResourceSchemaDeletedEvent payload fixed as (SchemaId, GroupId); spec edge case 'schema delete does not raise per-instance events'; AC-5 test asserts exactly one event.
chosen: Only ResourceSchemaDeletedEvent; consumer cascades by SchemaId

question: Should deleting a schema soft-delete the ResourceType row instead of hard-deleting it as today?
context: Owner stated in round 1 (free text): everything that is deleted must be a soft delete. Today DELETE /resources/types/{id} soft-deletes instances but HARD-deletes the ResourceType row (and its property definitions via DB cascade). GroupDeletedHandler also hard-deletes all types of a deleted group. ResourceType already has DeletedAt, a Delete(now) method and a global query filter, so soft delete is mostly wiring — but the unique index (GroupId, Name) would then block re-creating a schema with the name of a soft-deleted one unless the index is made partial (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL), which fits into the single migration of this story.

code_says.claim: ResourceType has DeletedAt, IsDeleted and Delete(DateTime now) but DeleteResourceTypeCommandHandler calls RemoveResourceType (EF Remove) instead.
Global query filter DeletedAt == null exists on ResourceType; unique index on (GroupId, Name) is not filtered.

options.label: Soft-delete in DELETE command only
options.consequences: Handler calls resourceType.Delete(now) then SaveChangesAsync; property definitions stay; unique index becomes partial (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) in the story's migration so the name can be reused. GroupDeletedHandler keeps hard-deleting (out of scope, as the story says).

options.label: Soft-delete in DELETE command and in GroupDeletedHandler
options.consequences: As above, plus GroupDeletedHandler switches from ExecuteDeleteAsync to ExecuteUpdateAsync(DeletedAt). Widens the story into the group-deletion path and its tests.

options.label: Keep hard delete as today
options.consequences: No behaviour change; only events are added. Contradicts the stated rule.

recommendation: Soft-delete in DELETE command only — it honours the rule where the story already touches code, reuses Delete(now) that exists, and the partial unique index rides on the migration this story needs anyway; the group-deletion path is explicitly out of scope and can follow the same rule in its own story.
argument_against: A rule that applies 'everywhere' but is implemented in one of two delete paths leaves the codebase inconsistent for an unknown time; doing both now costs one ExecuteUpdateAsync change and one test, and avoids a second story for a three-line fix.
consequences: If soft delete: new AC (schema delete keeps the row with DeletedAt; GET returns 404; name reusable), migration gains a partial unique index, ResourceSchemaDeletedEvent semantics unchanged. Evidence for the index change: F-8 (app-level check already excludes DeletedAt != null at CreateResourceTypeCommandDataProvider.cs:21; DB index unfiltered at ResourceTypeConfiguration.cs:17; HasFilter pattern at ManagementGroupConfiguration.cs:14). Existing hard-delete assertions at UpdateDeleteResourceTypeTests.cs:185/:283 must be rewritten.
